title: The tentmaker
hook: Paul supports himself making tents while he travels (Acts 18:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha and Mary: one sister busy serving, one sitting to listen. Your line was the better part. Did you leave one task undone for ten minutes? Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

The book of Acts is full of riots, shipwrecks and prison doors. Then, in Corinth, it slows down long enough to mention a job. A traveling teacher arrives in the city and finds a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, lately come from Italy. They share a trade. So he moves in with them, and he goes to work. A bench, his hands, the day's labor. Then, every sabbath, he goes to the synagogue to reason with whoever will listen. The man is Paul, and the book that tells his travels pauses to name his day job. Today's word is that job.
screen: `A JOB IN CORINTH.` → `A COUPLE WITH THE SAME TRADE.` → `A BENCH, THEN THE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: First, the verse itself, in the King James Bible: "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers." Wrought is the old word for worked. Paul isn't visiting a workshop. He's in it. Second, why he did it. Later in Acts, saying goodbye to friends from Ephesus, Paul holds up his hands: "Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me." In his own letters he explains more. He says he had a right to be supported by the people he taught, and chose not to use it, so that nothing would hinder the gospel and he could offer it without charge. The message was free, so he paid his own way. Third, what the text leaves out. Acts doesn't describe the work at all: no tools, no customers, no hours. It names the trade and moves on. What it makes plain is that the teacher worked, and that he wasn't ashamed to say so. Fourth, the people beside him. Aquila and Priscilla aren't just landlords. In Acts and in Paul's letters they appear again as teachers and friends, partners in the work as much as in the trade. Some Christians today borrow the word itself. They call someone a tentmaker when they carry their faith into an ordinary job and pay their own way, rather than being paid to preach. Paul's letters also thank the church at Philippi for gifts sent to him, so he did sometimes accept help. But in Corinth, Acts shows him at the bench. He worked with his hands.
screen: `OF THE SAME CRAFT, HE WROUGHT.` · `THESE HANDS HAVE MINISTERED.` · `THE MESSAGE FREE, HIS OWN WAY PAID.` · `PARTNERS AT THE BENCH.` · then, large: `BY THEIR OCCUPATION THEY WERE TENTMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing in your life that someone else quietly pays for or does for you. A ride, a bill, a meal, a chore you've let drift onto someone else's plate. No guilt, just notice it. Then ask what one piece of it you could take back this week. Breathe with that. If you pray, you can offer your hands and their work in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
The tentmaker. Paul's trade, according to Acts: working with Aquila and Priscilla, paying his own way while he taught. Today's word.
Your line: work with my hands. Today, pay your own way in one thing: cover your share, do your own chore, or make the thing instead of asking for it. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christians call working an ordinary job while sharing their faith 'tentmaking', after Paul in Acts 18.

fork.setup: you're Paul, arriving in Corinth with a message to share and a living to earn. what do you do?
options: ask the synagogue to support you.
find people of your trade and go to work.
wait for followers to offer you a home.
fork.reveal: Acts says he found Aquila and Priscilla, of the same craft, lived with them and worked, and taught on the sabbath.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul was a full-time preacher supported by churches.
what it means: Acts says he worked as a tentmaker, and Paul says he chose not to be paid by those he taught, so the gospel came without charge.
what a scholar hears: Acts names the trade without describing it, and some Christians now use 'tentmaker' for anyone who carries faith into an ordinary job.

notes: Claim to check: 'some scholars think the word could cover leather as well as cloth' (Greek skenopoios); hedged, no Greek given.
Claim to check: the modern use of 'tentmaker' for self-supporting Christian workers is attributed to 'some Christians today'.
The hook's 'needle, thread, heavy cloth or hide' is an image, not a textual claim; Acts doesn't describe the work.

Editor: cut the 'some scholars think leather as well as cloth' claim (teach, trapdoor) and the hook's cloth-or-hide image; cut unsourced 'busy port city', 'no patron, no salary', 'before he does anything else'; the 1 Corinthians 9 reason now follows the text (nothing to hinder the gospel, without charge) instead of 'in it for the money'; hook opener varied from the run of fragment-list openers; practice no longer repeats the hands-palms-up opening used on days 883, 887 and 896.

Audit (serious): 'Paul did not ask anyone to carry him' overstated the text; Philippians 4:15–16 and 2 Corinthians 11:8–9 show Paul accepted gifts from Philippi and other churches. Teach now says so and keeps self-support to Corinth and 1 Corinthians 9; trapdoor's 'paid his own way so the message was never for sale' tightened to what 1 Cor 9 says.
